title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known.
lead: This archive already had five registers for what it knows — the open questions, the research log, the sources, the method, and the corrections folded into each page. It had none for what it is doing. That lived in a chat window, which is the one place that does not survive the session, and on 15 September it cost a letter sent to a woman who had been thanked fourteen hours earlier. This is the register that answers who has to move next.
close: Everything here owned by David is a decision or a payment. Everything owned by this archive is work that can start without asking anybody. Everything blocked is waiting on a filing cabinet in South Africa, Portugal, Poland or Germany — or on one of five living people who were written to about a finding that concerns them.

rows.what: Confirm Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear as Derrick's biological father from a document, not an inference
rows.note: The DNA proves Derrick descends from **Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle as a couple** — 253 of the 297.5 cM he shares with his closest match lie outside every region he shares with any Castle cousin. The couple had **two sons**, and in June 1948 one was thirty-one and the other was eleven. What is missing is a record naming Leonard as anybody's father. Two death notices were requested from the Master at Cape Town on 15 September; see [the DNA page](/dna/).

rows.what: Master of the High Court, Cape Town — J294 death notices in estates 10761/2024 and 018561/2021
rows.note: Gillian Agnes Louisa Nel, born Wear, and Patricia Mary Maud Grant, born Wear. Each file holds a death notice with a field for the **father's full names**. Sent to Mr D Keyster, the estate controller for file numbers ending in 1. His auto-reply diverts only appointment queries, so a copy request should stay with him. Ms N Mphetshwa has left the section — that cc was wasted, and on 15 September her own auto-reply CONFIRMED it in her own words: "kindly note that I am no longer working at the Deceased Estate Appointment section". Mr Keyster's auto-reply also fired and diverts APPOINTMENT queries only, to Ms Portia Arendse — so a copy request correctly stays with him. Both confirmations, neither an answer. VINDICATED 15 September by row 33: six marriage registers across thirty years and two form designs have been read and NONE records a parent. The J294 death notice asks for the father's full names and the mother's maiden name, which makes this letter the best South African route to the one fact the archive cannot document — not a redundant one. ANSWERED 15 September at 09:57 — the first substantive reply on this row. Mr Keyster asks for a formal application on an attached form, APPLICATION FORM FOR COPIES.pdf, with proof of payment, submitted 'on groundfloor' at 45 Castle Street, Dullah Omar Building, Cape Town. That last part is an IN-PERSON instruction and David is in Australia — but Mr Keyster answered by email, so email submission may well be acceptable and must be asked rather than assumed. His reply also gives neither the fee nor the banking details, and nothing can be paid without them. A reply is drafted asking exactly those two things. The form itself is a PDF attachment this archive cannot open, so David has to read it. Replied the same hour, Gmail 1a0a482ea47212a0, asking the two questions and — deliberately — restating that David is not a relative and claims no interest in either estate, so that if his office limits copies to interested parties the refusal arrives before the money does.

rows.what: National Archives, Pretoria — four Luwinski court files, 1948 to 1951
rows.note: **WLD 2545/1950 — IVONE versus KURT, restitution of conjugal rights.** She sued him. That is the step a deserted spouse takes, and it sits between the divorce he filed in 1948 (**WLD 1950/1948**) and the one he filed in 1951 (**497/1951** and **2368/1951**). Four actions in three years, in both directions, with Derrick born in the middle of them. It hid because NAAIRS spells both names wrong — *Luwenski*, *Figaretto* — so every sweep missed it twice over. Sent to `Enquiries2@dsac.gov.za`, with 2545/1950 named as the one to do first.

rows.what: Henry Robert Wear's own estate, MHG 10245/69 — its death notice names his children
rows.note: This would test the whole Letchworth reconstruction against a South African record rather than an English index. **It cannot be emailed**: Ms Mavis Xaba of the Reading Room confirmed on 14 September that MHG files are *bound* and cannot be scanned. Added on 15 September to the commission the Lerena/Booyzen session already placed with a private researcher — same depot, same visit, and flagged as the least important of the seven.

rows.what: The two ante-nuptial contracts, June 1948 and February 1956
rows.note: Both marriages are recorded on the civil registers as entered into **WITH** an antenuptial contract, so the deeds exist. They sit in a **Deeds Registry**, which is a different institution from the archives and will not act on a letter or a telephone call. Stuck for weeks; on 15 September the researcher was asked whether she does that work or can name someone who does. AMENDED 15 September: there are THREE, not two. The Wear-Dunlop contract of 30 October 1951 was found the same evening by reading certificate 1397 at full resolution, and it is the only one of the three that names Leonard. Request 18 carries the correction and is held until the researcher replies.

rows.what: Four letters to living DNA matches, and one to a stranger about her own father
rows.note: Three went into threads opened in June 2025. The fourth — to the keeper of the seven-person tree that is the only source giving Leonard a mother called Castle — was **the first cold approach this archive has made**, and it tells a stranger that her father probably had a son she has never heard of. It also went to an account belonging to a woman who **died in March 2024**, so it may be read by her family or by nobody.

rows.what: GenDatabase — permission to publish six facts that came from them and nowhere else
rows.note: Their terms forbid republishing without written permission and this archive is on the open web. Submitted 15 September. **If refused**, those six facts come off the public pages into the working notes and the site will say a source asked for them to go, rather than deleting them quietly. It costs the argument nothing — the Wear reconstruction rests on English indexes and the Government Gazette, neither of which is theirs.

rows.what: Eleven institutional letters still unanswered — Berlin, Bydgoszcz, Koszalin, Maputo, Porto, Lisbon, Pretoria, Johannesburg
rows.owner: eight archives and two Masters' offices
rows.note: Two acknowledged: the Arquivo Histórico Militar in nine minutes, and Bydgoszcz with a warning that a complicated query can take over a month. Everything else is silence. See [the status page](/status/).

rows.what: Read the 1948 Johannesburg marriage register at full resolution
rows.note: Done 15 September. Read a third time, and this time from the archive's own microfilm rather than from a photograph in the family tree: digital film 008109682, frame 2047, image ark 3:1:3Q9M-CSJ1-SJQK. FamilySearch's own pages would not render — the session had been rate-limited to about one response every thirty-five seconds, which the site's front end shows as a hang — so the page was rebuilt locally from its 108 deep-zoom tiles and every cell magnified between four and five times, with the sideways columns rotated upright. One real correction: the couple's address is 108 DUNOTTAR Street, SYDENHAM, not Dunstan Street, Braamfontein. Everything the argument rests on holds, including the one that matters — column (10) reads With A.N.C. at 5.2x, four letters, not Without.

rows.what: Settle whether Leonard died in 1973 or 1979
rows.note: Worked hard on 15 September and not settled — but the evidence is now correctly weighed, which it was not before. Three routes failed. NAAIRS is down a second day, returning "The connection to the Search Manager Server is inactive" with an empty database list. Gazettes.Africa returns nothing for "Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear", "Wear, Leonard" or "L. A. R. Wear" in any year — and that proves nothing, because the control damns it: a search for Luwinski returns eight documents and not one is Kurt's own 1969 estate notice, which certainly existed. FamilySearch has both his marriages and no death record at all. What did change: GenDatabase's own profile page says in its own words that this record is INCOMPLETE as per their verification, and prints his date of birth as the corrupt string 0017. So 1979 is a damaged entry in a state index and 1973 is a daughter's family tree, and neither is a document. The archive should stop preferring 1979. The cheap way to close it is GenDatabase's single Verified Report at R20, which releases the identity number, the place of death and the full date — a purchase, so it is David's to make and not this archive's. NARROWED 15 September: he was alive on 13 SEPTEMBER 1969, buying his father's grave at West Park. That rules out nothing — both 1973 and 1979 are after it — but it is a hard floor, from a municipal record.

rows.what: Find whether Bruce Wallace Wear had sons — a Y test from one would end this in a single reading
rows.note: **Not reachable from the sources available, and kept here so nobody tries it again the same way.** A son of Bruce born in the 1960s would be in his sixties now, so he is not in a *death* database; and South African civil marriages on FamilySearch stop at **1974**, so a marriage in the 1980s or 1990s is not there either. GenDatabase cannot find living people. **The Y-test route needs contact with living Wears, not records** — which makes it a question for the people already written to, not a search. **Retested 15 September at the family's push**, by the one route left — Michelle Ann Wear, b.1978, d.2017 Johannesburg, whose estate would name her parents. **She is in no gazette and not in GenDatabase at all.** Two routes, both closed.

rows.what: Date the Wear family's emigration
rows.note: **Answered: they were gone before 29 September 1939.** The 1939 Register has seven Wears in Hertfordshire and the household is not among them, and a national search returns Henry Robert Wear in the 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921 censuses and then stops. The absence is real rather than redaction — born 1889 and 1895, he and Martha would be 137 and 131, so their records would be open if they existed. **One daughter stayed**: *Jeannett (E M) Wear, 1919, 18 Ridge Avenue, Letchworth*, aged twenty on register night. She followed later and died in South Africa in 2001.

rows.what: Re-run every woman in the archive by maiden name
rows.note: **Run, and the useful answer is a negative.** Ivone is in **no South African death record under any name she used** — not Salkow, not Luwinski, not de Witt, not Figueiredo, and no Ivone among the six women in the verified deaths carrying that maiden name. She married three times in that country and died out of its reach. **That is what dying in Porto looks like from this side**, and it is the first corroboration this archive has for a death it has never been able to date.

rows.what: Big Y-700 on Derrick's kit
rows.note: A purchase, and **this archive does not spend other people's money.** It would place him on a branch young enough for a surname to mean something. Of the 7,748 public members of the R-U106 project only 34 sit under R-S11477, whose common ancestor lived around 200 BCE — so the surnames on that branch are ninety generations away and mean nothing at all. SHARPENED 15 September by row 45. The argument for the Big Y is no longer 'more detail'. The classic haplotree shows forty-two branches below R-S11477, and its two immediate children are R-Z27559 and R-BY42072 — and R-BY42072 is TAGGED ENGLAND, as is R-FT370170 below it (13 testers, c. 550 CE). The Y evidence has so far only been able to say NOT ASHKENAZI. A Big Y that landed Derrick on one of those two branches would make it say something positive and geographically pointed for the first time.

rows.what: Whether Derrick should be told before any more strangers are
rows.note: Raised twice and overruled twice, which is the family's decision and not this archive's to make — but it is recorded here because it is still live. Five living people have now been written to about a finding that concerns a man who has not, so far as this archive knows, been told that his family is writing to them.

rows.what: Two archives share one mailbox, and neither knew what the other had sent
rows.note: The cause of the duplicate letter. `Projects/SHARED-CONTACTS.md` now sits in **both** this archive's notes and the Lerena/Booyzen one, listing every shared contact and its live state, every address known to be dead and why, and the constraints that apply to both. One rule at the top: **before writing to any institution, search the sent mail.**

rows.what: Track what comes back, not only what goes out
rows.note: The tracker recorded what was *sent* and never what was *said back*, so Ms Xaba's reply — that MHG files are bound and cannot be emailed — sat unread for a day while this archive went on framing every estate request as *just send me the one page*. There is now a **What has actually come back** table on [the status page](/status/).

rows.what: Order Edwina Ann Wear's estate, 33157/2014, for the parents named in its death notice
rows.note: **Founded on a mistake, and kept here rather than deleted.** A full day went into Edwina as Derrick's possible half-sister. She was born **Edwina Ann GREEN** and married Bruce Wallace Wear — Leonard's younger brother — in 1980. A Wear by marriage, no blood relation at all. Every dead end around her had been the answer saying so: her parents were unfindable under Wear because they were Greens, and she was still a Wear at 69 because it was her married name.

rows.what: Find the Halsey marriage that joins the Brown and Castle families to the surname on the closest match's card
rows.note: **Founded on a mistake.** A week went into the surname *Halsey* because it was the name printed on a DNA match card. It was the wrong half of a married couple: the 1952 register gives the birthplaces as **Cape Province** for him and **ENGLAND** for her, and the English link was the wife. There was never a Halsey marriage to find, which is exactly why the England and Wales index came back empty.

rows.what: Correct the archive's own errors in public rather than editing them away
rows.note: Standing work, and the reason this archive is worth anything. Published corrections to date: the Castles were **Hertfordshire, not Norfolk**; Caroline was a **Wallis**, not a Walls, and the tree was right where this archive was wrong; Derrick's birth year leaked onto the DNA page and was removed; the generation claim was walked back within the hour; and Henrique was called the son of a marriage that the 1948 register proves never happened.

rows.what: Mervin Halsey's parents — the Henry George Charles and Mary Ellen guess
rows.note: **Founded on two birth years and killed by a third date.** This archive proposed Henry George Charles Halsey (1906–1993) and Mary Ellen Halsey (d.1981) as Mervin's parents because they were the right ages. But **he married Evelyn Ruth in 1932** and **Mervin was born on 15 June 1930** — two years earlier; Mary Ellen has no spouse recorded and is not his wife; and Mervin was born in the **Cape Province**, which nothing places any of them in. Off the critical path regardless: the Halsey line stopped mattering the moment column four of the 1952 register was read.

rows.what: What is filed behind marriage entry 858 of 1948 — and the back of the sheet
rows.note: Drafted as request 15 and DELIBERATELY NOT SENT. The plan was a letter to Home Affairs. Searching the sent mail first — the rule written after the Xaba duplication — turned up a reply from a professional South African researcher in May 2020 saying that certificates of any kind, abridged, unabridged or vault, can only be applied for IN PERSON at Home Affairs, that third-party applications are no longer accepted, and that an applicant living overseas must go through the South African Embassy or Consulate in their country. So the letter as conceived would have gone to an address that cannot act on it — the fourth dead address of this project, avoided this time before sending rather than after a bounce. It is redrafted to the High Commission in Canberra and asks HOW rather than asking for the record. And it surfaces something uncomfortable: if eligibility really is limited to immediate family, then for the 1948 marriage that means the two spouses, both long dead, and their son of record. This document cannot be got without Derrick, which collides with row 15. Raised once, here, and left with David.

rows.what: The reverse of the 1948 marriage register — the form says P.T.O. and nobody has turned it over
rows.note: Struck 15 September, with an answer rather than a shrug. The film viewer loaded once the throttle eased, and the frames either side of ours were opened: frame 2046 is certificate 764, Louw and Swanepoel; frame 2048 is certificate 295, Mowbray and Gemmer. Both are certificate FRONTS, both 19 June 1948. The film runs front, front, front across its 3,228 images. So the reverse of the sheet was never photographed, and no amount of patience with FamilySearch will produce it. The question is not dropped — it is folded into row 22, because the letter to Home Affairs about entry 858 has to ask for both sides of it now.

rows.what: The Wear–Dunlop ante-nuptial contract, Johannesburg, October 1951
rows.note: Found tonight by reading the register of Leonard's second marriage at full resolution: certificate 1397 of 1951, column 10, reads "with". So a notarial ante-nuptial contract was executed for Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear and Marjorie Eileen Dunlop, born Walker, and registered in the Johannesburg Deeds Office. This is the third ANC on the archive's list, after Kurt's two, and it is the only one of the three that names LEONARD. An ANC recites each party's full particulars and is not confined to the register's eleven columns, which makes it the best document about him this archive has ever had a route to. Goes to the Pretoria researcher with rows 4 and 5.

rows.what: Leonard's Second World War service record — SANDF Documentation Centre, Pretoria
rows.note: New tonight, from the 1940 marriage register: Leonard's occupation is entered as ARMY and his residence as ROBERTS HEIGHTS, PRETORIA — the Union Defence Force's principal base — on 7 September 1940, one year and one day after South Africa entered the war. Second World War service records are held by the SANDF Documentation Centre in Pretoria, and an attestation form gives full name, date and place of birth, next of kin and in most cases THE NAMES OF THE PARENTS. That is exactly what the archive is missing. The entire chain rests on Leonard being a son of Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, and the only source saying so is a seven-person tree built by his daughter. An attestation form would turn that into a government record. SENT as request 16. Three things settled first. This mailbox already has an unanswered enquiry from David, sent 9 September for the sibling archive about the Booyzen family, so the draft opens by naming it — two cold letters in six days is how the Xaba duplication happened. The address the whole internet gives, sandfdoc@mweb.co.za, is DEAD: it bounced on 9 September with Relay access denied, and the Centre has moved from Visagie Street to Irene; archive@dod.mil.za is the live one. And he was almost certainly NOT an officer — officers were gazetted by full name, the control searches return their entries, and Leonard returns nothing under six spellings — so the letter asks for an attestation and a medal-roll entry rather than a commission. SENT 15 September to archive@dod.mil.za, Gmail 1a0a3b70c6389154.

rows.what: The Catholic marriage register at Rosebank, 7 September 1940 — Archdiocese of Johannesburg
rows.note: The civil registers have no parents' columns. Catholic sacramental registers do. Leonard and Phyllis were married at Rosebank by W. P. Whelan, who filled in the Denomination line himself as "Catholic Priest", and they were married BY BANNS rather than on a licence — so the intention was read in church on three Sundays and generates its own entry as well. A parish marriage register of 1940 ordinarily names the father and mother of both parties. This is a church record, so it sits entirely outside the Home Affairs eligibility problem in request 15. Identify the Rosebank parish in the Archdiocese of Johannesburg and write to it. SENT as request 17. The parish is the Church of the Immaculate Conception, 16 Keyes Avenue, Rosebank, established 1936 — four years before the wedding. Not asserted as certain: the civil register gives only the word Rosebank, so the letter asks to be redirected if the marriage belongs to another parish or to a chaplaincy at the Roberts Heights camp. Both letters disclose plainly that David is not a descendant and makes no claim to be. SENT 15 September to Info@rosebankcatholicchurch.co.za, Gmail 1a0a3b72c965ecf1.

rows.what: Leonard's own birth certificate, GRO, Hitchin, first quarter 1917
rows.note: THE OBVIOUS DOCUMENT THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER ORDERED, and it should be embarrassing that it took until now. Every route tried this week has been an attempt to get Leonard's parents out of a SOUTH AFRICAN record — marriage registers with no parents' columns, an estate that does not exist, a military file, a parish book. His ENGLISH BIRTH CERTIFICATE names his father and mother outright. The index entry is already held: WEAR, Leonard A R, Hitchin, Q1 1917. A GRO certificate costs about GBP 12.50 and arrives as a PDF in days. If it names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, the single weakest link in the whole chain — that Leonard is their son, currently resting on a seven-person family tree built by his daughter — becomes a government record. A purchase, so David's, but this is the cheapest decisive document on the entire list.

rows.what: The Wear-Castle marriage certificate, GRO, Hitchin, fourth quarter 1914
rows.note: The companion to the row above, and the generation behind it. The archive established that the ONLY Wear-Castle marriage in the whole English index is Henry R Wear to Martha L Castle, Hitchin Q4 1914. The certificate names BOTH FATHERS, with their occupations. That does two things at once: it confirms the couple from a state record rather than an inference, and it pushes the line back a generation on both sides at a stroke. Same cost, same speed.

rows.what: All six Wear children, from the GRO index on the mother's maiden name
rows.note: DONE — and the row should never have been written. It claimed the sibship had been cited repeatedly while only four of the six were named. That was false: section 7 of the Wear notes names all six with quarter and district, from FindMyPast's England & Wales Births searched on mother's maiden name CASTLE — six results, all Hitchin. Leonard A R Q1 1917, Janette E M Q4 1919, Kathleen E Q1 1921, Cynthia Y E Q2 1931, Linda A Q2 1933, Bruce W Q3 1936. Closed with the reason attached rather than deleted: the work list exists to stop the archive re-doing work, and a row written without re-reading the notes does the opposite.

rows.what: Name the second son, and find out what became of him
rows.note: DONE, and it produced the most important thing on the list. The second son was already named — BRUCE WALLACE WEAR, Q3 1936 Hitchin, in South Africa by 1959, four marriages and three divorces in the Witwatersrand. What was NOT known is whether he is dead. The notes said "Bruce was gone by 2014", inferred from his wife Edwina's estate notice naming no surviving spouse. Tested against two indexes on 15 September: the Verified Death Database holds Edwina and NOT Bruce; the Government Gazette estate notices hold Edwina and NOT Bruce. And the inference has an obvious alternative — he had already divorced three wives, so a fourth divorce leaves her with no surviving spouse while he lives. Absence is not proof of life and he could have died abroad. But the honest position is now 'not recorded as dead in South Africa', not 'gone by 2014'. See row 31: born 1936 he would be ninety, and he is not a cousin — he is LEONARD'S BROTHER, a direct male-line son of Henry Robert Wear.

rows.what: Is there a living male-line Wear who could take a Y test?
rows.note: SHARPENED 15 September, and it now has a name. The candidate is not a distant cousin to be hunted: it is BRUCE WALLACE WEAR, Leonard's younger brother, born Q3 1936, who carries the same Y chromosome the archive is trying to match against Derrick's R-S11477. Row 30 establishes that he is not recorded as dead in South Africa. If he is living he is ninety. ONE Y-37 test from him confirms or destroys this entire investigation in a single reading, for a fraction of the Big Y in row 14. He is a living person: nothing about him goes on the site beyond the index entry already published, and THIS ARCHIVE WILL NOT APPROACH HIM. Whether anybody does is David's, and it walks straight into row 15.

rows.what: The 1953 Salkow marriage register, read at full resolution
rows.note: DONE 15 September. Certificate 146 of 1953, Johannesburg, frame 1087, image 3:1:3Q9M-CSV4-R9JG-K, rebuilt from 336 tiles. Morris Isaac Salkow, 31, born Transvaal, DIVORCEE, salesman. Ivone Luwinski formerly de Witt born de Figueredo, 25, Portuguese East Africa, DIVORCEE, SALESLADY, of 9 Rudney Road, Rossmore. Without ante-nuptial contract; special licence 220116; and ORDER FILED against BOTH names — which is the second document, and the first she signed, proving the 1951 divorce from Kurt was actually granted. Salkow turns out to have married three times, 1943, 1953 and 1960, so this marriage ended too. AND IT CORRECTED THIS ARCHIVE THE SAME DAY: the age panel published on /1948/ that morning read the February and June 1948 ages as a two-year jump in four months. With the 1953 figure the real shape is a stated age drifting steadily YOUNGER — 22, then 24, then 25 where 1924 requires 28 or 29. The panel is rewritten, and the rule it now carries is that no inference in this archive may rest on an age Ivone gave a clerk.

rows.what: Find a South African marriage form that DOES have a parents' column
rows.note: ANSWERED, and the answer is NO. The South African civil marriage register never asked for parents — not in any decade and not on either form. The archive had read five (1940, 1948, 1951, 1952 eleven-column; 1956 on the fourteen-field B.M.D. 3(a)). A genuine 1970 register was pulled and read to test whether a later redesign added them: image 3:1:3QS7-L9Z5-GQPP, entry no. 2 of 1970, form B.M.D. 3. Its fourteen fields are names, date, solemnized at, identity number, race, age and date of birth, ante-nuptial contract, personal status, occupation, place of birth, address, banns or licence, consent, remarks. Not one is a parent. The state asked more and more about the parties themselves and never once asked whose children they were.

rows.what: Gillian's 1969 marriage register, Heather's 1968, Patricia's 1997
rows.note: STRUCK by row 33 the same evening it was proposed. It existed only on the hope that a later marriage form named parents, which would have made Gillian's 1969 register do for free what the Master of the High Court is being asked to do. The 1970 form has fourteen fields and no parents, so these three registers will not name Leonard and there is no point ordering them for that purpose.

rows.what: Re-read the 1952 Halsey-Wear register for the columns nobody looked at
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it paid. The sheet had been opened once, for column 4, which redirected the whole archive; nobody went back for the rest. Certificate 51 of 1952, frame 2149, image 3:1:3Q9M-CSJY-YGDD. Three things came out. (1) 64 GREENFIELD ROAD, GREENSIDE, JOHANNESBURG — Cynthia's address at 21 and a spinster, so very probably the household address of Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, and the first address this archive has ever had for them. (2) Banns, at St Martin's-in-the-Veld, denomination ANGLICAN CHURCH — so the Wears were Anglican, and the 1940 Catholic ceremony came from Phyllis's side, which is what request 17 guessed and now has evidence for. (3) Column 10 reads WITH, a FOURTH ante-nuptial contract. And one disappointment worth recording: column 9, Consent given by, reads 'Own' for both — had Cynthia been a minor it would have carried her father's name outright.

rows.what: Estate-notice sweep: Martha Maud Wear 1986, and every Wear estate 1965-1990
rows.note: DONE 15 September by driving NAAIRS itself rather than a mirror of it. THE SWEEP FOUND NO WEAR ESTATE IN THE TRANSVAAL BETWEEN 1970 AND 1976; the last is the father's, MHG 10245/69, remarks SURVIVING SPOUSE MARTHA MAUD WEAR. Martha Maud's own 1986 estate is NOT absent — it is out of range, because the deceased-estate index runs to the end of 1976 and stops (2,246 estate records in 1976, one in 1977, zero after). That has to be got from the Master's office direct, which is row 2's correspondence. The measurement is the real result: it makes Leonard's two published death years asymmetric for the first time — 1973 is INSIDE the index and he is not in it; 1979 is three years past its last year and cannot be tested at all. Published on /leonard/ with the limits stated.

rows.what: Sweep the Government Gazette for Leonard the engineer
rows.note: He gave his occupation as ENGINEER in 1951. Gazettes.Africa is free, full-text, and the tooling is already written. Sweep for company directorships, business transfers under section 34, insolvencies, tenders, and government appointments. Expectations should be low and the OCR is poor — but the Piccadilly Hat Company came out of exactly this kind of sweep and it opened Kurt's entire working life.

rows.what: Kurt's naturalisation, and a plain answer about whether such lists exist at all
rows.note: DONE 15 September, both halves, and the plain answer is YES THE LISTS EXIST AND NO KURT IS NOT IN THEM. The Government Gazette publishes naturalisation in two series — intention-to-apply notices under section 10 of the South African Citizenship Act 1949, and lists of certificates actually issued; 246 gazettes carry the heading and both were read in full for 1975 and 1976 while working row 58. A full-text search of every South African gazette returns LUWINSKI exactly eight times and this archive had already read all eight — six Piccadilly Hat Company partnership notices, the 1972 Paula application and the 1975 Pallou's Dress Centre notice. NONE IS A NATURALISATION NOTICE. Luwinski is a rare surname and the same search demonstrably finds him, so unlike the WEAR null this one is worth something. NAAIRS cannot help: a search of the central-government database for NATURALIZATION returns 342 documents and every one is a POLICY FILE OR A BILL — the 1926 Act, its 1927 amendment, South West Africa bills. Individual naturalisation files are not indexed at item level anywhere this archive can reach, so the remaining route is a letter, which is row 61.

rows.what: Sweep CASTLE through the South African record the way WEAR was swept
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it returned a coincidence that has to be handled rather than filed. TAB WLD 155/1915 and 329/1919: DIVORCE, MAUD MABEL LONGHURST (BORN CASTLE) VERSUS AUBREY LEONARD — the index writes the defendant by forenames alone because the surname is shared, and TAB MHG 3632/50 gives him in full as AUBREY LEONARD LONGHURST, died 1950, second wife Athalie born van Aardt. SO: A WOMAN CALLED MAUD, BORN CASTLE, MARRIED TO A MAN CALLED AUBREY LEONARD, IN JOHANNESBURG, TWO YEARS BEFORE LEONARD AUBREY ROBERT WEAR WAS BORN TO MARTHA MAUD CASTLE. Three elements of this archive's central identity in one line. It is probably nothing: Martha Maud was nineteen in 1915, married in Hertfordshire since 1914 and on the 1921 census at Letchworth, so she is not the plaintiff, and both Castle and Maud are common. BUT IT WOULD ANSWER A QUESTION NOBODY HERE HAS ASKED OUT LOUD — WHY JOHANNESBURG? Emigrating families go where somebody already is, and if Maud Mabel Castle was Martha Maud's aunt or elder cousin then the Castle family had a Johannesburg branch twenty years before the Wears arrived, and a boy christened Leonard Aubrey in 1917 was named after his mother's relative's husband. NOTHING IS CLAIMED. Written up in castle-baldock.md with the caution attached, because a later reader who found these three references without it could do real damage. Also swept: WEAR+CASTLE returns zero across all repositories — no South African record joins the two names.

rows.what: Leonard's grave — and with it, probably, the death year
rows.note: WORKED and came back empty, which is itself worth having. Searched the FamilySearch collection that holds both his parents — South Africa, Gauteng, Johannesburg, Cemetery Records 1840-2019 — plus every South African death, burial and Find a Grave collection. LEONARD AUBREY ROBERT WEAR APPEARS EXACTLY TWICE IN ALL OF FAMILYSEARCH'S SOUTH AFRICAN HOLDINGS: his 1940 marriage and his 1951 marriage. No death, no burial, no grave. That is a real negative rather than a gap in the index, because the same collections hold Henry Robert at West Park in 1969, Martha Maud in 1986, Edwina in 2014 and Michelle in 2017. The likeliest reading is that he did not die in Johannesburg — he was divorced twice and could have gone anywhere. Which points straight back at row 10: GenDatabase's PLACE OF DEATH field is paywalled, and the R20 report would say which province to search. Blocked on that purchase, which is David's.

rows.what: Put Leonard at an address in every year the record allows
rows.note: WORKED to the end of what can be done from here, and the answer is that he cannot be placed. Three addresses in fifty-eight years: 72 Pix Road Letchworth in 1921, Roberts Heights Pretoria in September 1940, Polana Court Abel Road Berea in October 1951. BETWEEN 1941 AND 1950 THERE IS NOTHING AT ALL — no address, one recorded fact, that a daughter was born in 1941 — and 1948 sits in the middle of that hole. Nothing places Leonard in Johannesburg in 1948 except that he married there in 1940 and again in 1951, which is an inference from either side of a gap. The gazette route is now exhausted: full-text searches for Polana Court, Dunottar Street, Abel Road and Greenfield Road against the surname return nothing, and the only two hits for Greenfield Road and Wear are advertisements for ladies' wear. What is left — street and telephone directories, the Deeds Office property index, the voters rolls — all need somebody physically in Johannesburg or Pretoria, and none of them costs a fee worth arguing about. Added to the held brief for the researcher. Published on /leonard/ with the silences given the same weight as the entries. SUPERSEDED IN PART the same evening: a fourth address and a fourth fixed point — 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands, 13 September 1969, from the West Park grave register, folio W 8. Leonard was alive and in Johannesburg on that date, which is the last certain sighting the archive has of him.

rows.what: Date the emigration exactly, from the outward passenger lists
rows.note: Row 12 is marked done, and it is done only in the sense that the emigration is BOUNDED — after the 1921 census, before 29 September 1939. The UK outward passenger lists, BT27, would give the actual ship and the actual date. Two notes have carried this as a to-do for days without anyone touching it. It also answers something the archive has never asked: did Leonard travel WITH his parents, or separately, and at what age.

rows.what: Sort every match in the cluster into Wear side, Castle side, or neither
rows.note: DONE 15 September, by ratio rather than by segments, and the limits are published with it. For each shared match, cM-with-Derrick divided by cM-with-Penelope-Browne measures how much of that person's relationship to Derrick is left unexplained by the documented Castle line. All ten shared matches ranked. CATHERINE HALSEY 3.62, DARREN SEARLES 3.32, Jamie Morris 1.96, Josh Barnett 0.97, then the Browne core at 0.10 to 0.42. Searles is in neither of the tables the archive built on 14 September: 96.0 cM with Derrick and only 28.9 with the Castle descendant. On the reasoning that found the Wear line, that is what a Wear-side cousin looks like. Caveats stated on the page: the ratio conflates 'not on Browne's line' with 'distant from Browne', and the denominator is inflated at the bottom because those five are Browne's own first cousins. The bottom of the table is nearly meaningless; the top is not.

rows.what: Triangulate the 253 cM that are NOT Castle
rows.note: The same evidence from the other end. Those segments come from the WEAR side of the couple. Any other match who shares them is a Wear cousin. That is the group worth writing to, and the group most likely to contain a male-line Wear for row 31. STARTED 15 September and stopped at a known point. The candidate is DARREN SEARLES, and his match page confirms EIGHT shared segments with Derrick — but the coordinates sit behind the chromosome browser's Advanced options panel and did not come out of the DOM on this pass. The test is to ask how many of those eight fall inside the 253 cM of non-Castle regions: chromosomes 1 twice, 6, 7, 8, 12, 15, 18, 20 and 22 twice. If most do, the Wear line has a second living witness. Small next action, clearly defined.

rows.what: Re-check R-U106 for a Wear, Weir or Ware under S11477
rows.note: STANDING CHECK, and the date is the point. Checked 14 September, re-checked 15 September: R-U106 unchanged at 34 of 7,748, and STILL NO WEAR, WEIR OR WARE anywhere on the branch — the same five surname projects as yesterday (Ballew 16/62, Stafford 8/96, Blakely 8/68, Byrd 5/102, York 4/85). A dated negative is worth more than an undated one. BUT the re-check found a project the first pass missed: R1b-P89.2, where 33 OF 62 PUBLIC MEMBERS SIT ON DERRICK'S EXACT BRANCH — 53 per cent, against 0.4 per cent in R-U106. If a surname ever surfaces from the Y side it will surface there, and this archive was watching the wrong project. Re-check both, monthly, and record the date each time.

rows.what: A page for Leonard
rows.note: DONE 15 September. /leonard/ is live and in the menu. His life as far as it is documented, with every row tagged documented, inferred or disputed; the case that he is Derrick's biological father; and THE CASE AGAINST SET OUT AT THE SAME LENGTH, which is the point of the page. Row 50 is folded into it as a section rather than scattered elsewhere.

rows.what: Draw the segments, instead of describing them
rows.note: The 44-against-253 argument is the strongest thing in this archive and it is currently three paragraphs of prose. It is a picture: chromosomes along an axis, Derrick's shared segments with the closest match in one colour, the Castle cousins' in another, and the overlap visible or not visible at a glance. Anyone who sees it understands the argument in five seconds. Anyone who reads the prose has to take it on trust. DONE 15 September: the chromosome map is live on /dna/, computed at build time from the segment coordinates rather than typed in, so the 297.5 / 44.3 / 253.2 figures in the prose are derived from the data beside them. Matches labelled by role only; the copy in site/src/data has the surname keys stripped.

rows.what: Re-verify every address in SHARED-CONTACTS.md, and do it before writing, not after
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the old rule is replaced rather than reaffirmed. All twenty-six addresses this project has used were re-resolved and audited against the six that have actually failed. MX CAUGHT ONE OF THE SIX. The reason is now understood and published: dac.gov.za and dsac.gov.za resolve to the SAME mail gateway, so a renamed department keeps a perfectly valid MX record and the rejection happens inside, where DNS cannot see it. A live MX proves a mail server answers for the domain and nothing about the department, the office or the person. The replacement procedure, ordered by what actually catches things: search the sent mail first for prior contact AND prior bounces (three catches so far); prefer an address the institution itself gave you over a directory entry; check the institution still exists under that name and at that address; MX last, for a mistyped subdomain; then watch a day for a bounce. Written into SHARED-CONTACTS.md in both archives and published on /letters/.

rows.what: A follow-up calendar for nineteen unanswered letters
rows.note: DONE 15 September. /letters/ is live and in the menu, built from site/src/data/letters.json and RECOMPUTED ON EVERY BUILD, so the dates are live rather than written down once and forgotten. Fifteen letters, each with an interval chosen for the recipient rather than one global number: 10 days for a commissioned researcher who has been asked for rates, 21 for a Master's office or a national archive or a parish, 28 for an overseas archive in another language. Sorted by soonest due. The page says plainly why it exists — this archive had already sent one correspondent two emails in four hours and another a duplicate enquiry it had forgotten making.

rows.what: Write down what would DISPROVE Leonard
rows.note: DONE 15 September, as a section of the new Leonard page rather than a page of its own. Six things are named that would make this archive abandon the identification — a birth certificate naming different parents, a male-line Wear Y test that does not match R-S11477, an attestation form with a different next of kin, a third son in the birth index, a J294 naming a different father, and evidence he was out of the country in 1948. Written down BEFORE the documents arrive and published, so it cannot be quietly revised afterwards.

rows.what: Read the reverse of the 1951 and 1940 registers — or prove they were not filmed either
rows.note: ANSWERED 15 September, and now established across THREE separate films rather than assumed from one. Film 008109682 (the 1948 register): frames 2046 and 2048 are certificates 764 and 295, both fronts. Film 008161359 (the 1940 register, frame 473, certificate 13): frame 474 is an Afrikaans certificate from Turffontein, number 206 — a front. Film 008019258 (the 1951 register, frame 2700, certificate 1397): frame 2701 is certificate 1400, Siegbert Buchholz of Germany — a front. THE REVERSES OF THESE SHEETS WERE NEVER PHOTOGRAPHED. It is systematic to the collection's filming, not a quirk of one reel, and no amount of patience with FamilySearch will produce them. That strengthens request 15: whatever is written on the back of any of these registers survives only in the original bound books at Home Affairs.

rows.what: The Momple and Robertson line, so that Phyllis stops being a name
rows.note: BROKEN OPEN 15 September, after sitting untouched because Momple was a name with nothing attached. One NAAIRS query attached a family. TAB WLD 3046/1959: DIVORCE, LOUIS JAMES MOMPLE ROBERTSON VERSUS FLORENCE PERTHINIA — A JOHANNESBURG MAN CARRYING MOMPLE AS A MIDDLE NAME AND ROBERTSON AS A SURNAME, which is the classic signature of a mother's maiden name carried forward and exactly the joint this archive needed, since Phyllis Agnes ROBERTSON's mother was a MOMPLE. He is very probably her brother or first cousin. And behind him a whole family with estates: MHG 6060/50 MOMPLE, LOUIS ARTHUR, surviving spouse DORA MOMPLE BORN CARLSE; MHG 695/64 Dora Momple; TPD 1468/1950 Douglas Arthur Momple in re the late Louis Arthur Momple; and three daughters married out as Archer, Ackhurst and Gervais. MHG 6060/50 IS INSIDE THE ESTATE INDEX'S RANGE AND CAN BE ORDERED — its death notice names Louis Arthur Momple's parents and its estate file lists his children. If Phyllis's mother is among them, row 52 is answered and the Mauritian line behind her opens with it.

rows.what: Ask the Pretoria researcher about the 1951 ante-nuptial contract too
rows.note: WORKED, and the row turned out to be WRONG. It said to send a short amendment rather than let it sit. Reading the thread first showed the researcher already has two emails from 15 September — the Sunday brief at 23:15 and an addition at 03:25 that ALREADY asks the Deeds Registry question and names the 1948 and 1956 contracts — and has replied to neither, and has not said whether she takes the work at all. Our own second letter says in its first paragraph that everything in it can wait until she has answered about rates. A third email the same day would contradict that sentence, and would cost nothing to avoid, because she cannot go to the Deeds Registry before terms are agreed. DRAFTED AS REQUEST 18 AND HELD, to be appended to the reply when she answers rather than sent on its own. This is exactly what row 49 is for.

rows.what: John Anderson Wear, buried at West Park — who is he?
rows.note: STRUCK within the hour, and it is worth saying why. The Find a Grave record's PLACE field offers five candidate cemeteries for the ambiguous string 'West Park Cemetery' — Johannesburg, Cleveland Ohio, Long Eaton Derbyshire, Hereford Texas, and Bulawayo — and FamilySearch surfaced the Johannesburg one only because the query was filtered to South Africa. The record's own Country, State, County and City fields resolve to UNITED STATES OF AMERICA / TEXAS / DEAF SMITH / HEREFORD. He also appears as a father in Illinois births of 1883. He is an American and has nothing to do with this family. A place-name collision in an index, caught before anything was published — which is the first time this week that has happened before rather than after.

rows.what: 64 Greenfield Road, Greenside — find out who lived there
rows.note: DONE 15 September — overtaken rather than answered, and the detour was worth more than the row. The gazette gives nothing for 64 Greenfield Road, so instead of hunting the address the CEMETERY REGISTERS were opened, on the reasoning that a burial register records where the dead lived and a grave register records who BOUGHT the grave. Both are true. West Park Cemetery Private Graves Register, folio W 8 (published here first as W58; corrected the same evening): purchaser WEAR, Mr L. A. R., of 271 WILSON STREET, FAIRLANDS, receipt 11484, 13 September 1969, sixty pounds, grave 56045 section E.C., person buried HENRY ROBERT WEAR. Read at five times magnification the initial is a cursive L, not a J. And the 1986 burial register gives Martha Maud, aged 90, died at the Hillcrest Geriatric Centre, usual residence 12 and a half Second Street, PARKHURST — buried in grave 56045, the same grave. Row 55's own question is still unanswered; it has been overtaken, because the archive now has an address for LEONARD, which is what it actually wanted.

rows.what: Henrique’s Portuguese military record — now at the Arquivo Geral do Exército
rows.owner: the Arquivo Geral do Exército, Lisboa
rows.note: A reply came in at 06:54 on 15 September and was sitting unread. Maria Joao Pires, Coordinator of the Arquivo da Defesa Nacional, writes that for military records one must contact the ARQUIVO GERAL DO EXERCITO, arqgex@exercito.pt — a different body from the Arquivo Historico Militar this archive had already written to. Written to the same hour, citing the referral by name and date, Gmail 1a0a40447162eada. The prize is the same as it always was: a Portuguese military recenseamento names the father AND the mother of the man recensed, and Henrique's father is unknown. Row 33 makes this more important, not less — the South African civil registers have no parentage field at all, so the Portuguese paperwork is the only route left for him. Acknowledged the same day at 07:42: "Confirma-se a receção da sua correspondência eletrónica a qual será tratada pelos nossos serviços." So the referral address works. An acknowledgement, not an answer.

rows.what: Who authorised the second burial in grave 56045 in 1986
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that THE RECORD WAS NEVER MADE. Four more West Park images were rebuilt tile by tile. (1) The full two-page spread of Martha Maud's 1986 burial, folio W 104, image 3:1:3QHV-B3PY-2FKN, 7,407 x 3,164, 377 tiles: cause NATURAL CAUSES, burial order 37640, 17.3.86, undertaker REG, receipt 61610, R70.00, nature of interment "New Reopen." — and the Remarks column, which is where an authority would be noted, is EMPTY for her row. Not illegible, not cropped: empty. (2) The index side of the Private Graves folio, image 3:1:3QHV-13P1-89VT, read line by line across three magnified passes, holds exactly ONE Wear: Henry Robert, 13.9.69, grave 5604/5, Fol. W56. MARTHA MAUD IS NOT IN IT. A 1986 interment into a 1969 private grave generated no new private-grave entry, which is itself the explanation for the blank Remarks column: the reopening was handled as a burial, not as a grave transaction, so nobody had to sign for it. The row closes with the reason attached, not struck. What is left is the undertaker's own file — the register names REG — or Martha Maud's estate at the Master of the High Court, and neither is worth a row until the Master answers what it already has. THE DETOUR PAID AGAIN, twice: burial register folio W 56 row 4 gives HENRY ROBERT WEAR's usual residence, 5 LIVINGSTONE CT., 4TH ST., PARKHURST — the first address ever recorded for him in South Africa — with address at time of death General Hospital Jhb., died 11.9.69 of BRONCHOPNEUMONIA aged 80, burial order 2894, undertaker Cooks, R15.00. And the folio number this archive published for the grave register was WRONG: it is W 8, not W58, confirmed three ways.

rows.what: 5 Livingstone Court, 4th Street, Parkhurst — run the parents' documented address
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it paid far beyond the address. One gazette query on "Livingstone Court" returned four South African hits; the 1965 and 1977 ones are other people, but GOVERNMENT GAZETTE 4620 OF 21 MARCH 1975, under NATURALIZATION NOTICES, carries: EVANS, Mrs Janette Eileen Maud, formerly Bailey, nee WEAR, saleslady, 5 LIVINGSTONE COURT, 28 VIERDE STRAAT/FOURTH STREET, PARKHURST, JOHANNESBURG. The OCR interleaves two columns and the entry had to be unpicked from its neighbour, so the page itself was read. And the grant followed in GAZETTE 5007 OF 12 MARCH 1976: R54033 - EVANS, Janette Eileen Maud, 28/10/19, England, Citizen of the U.K. and C., 30/10/75. THREE GAINS. (1) The Parkhurst address is corroborated from a wholly independent source six years later, with the building's street number added — the cemetery clerk's hand and the Government Printer's type agree. (2) The birth date 28 October 1919 falls inside GRO quarter Q4 1919, so the Hitchin birth and the Johannesburg naturalisation are the same woman without an assumption. (3) THE FAMILY STAYED BRITISH: Leonard's eldest sister was still a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies in 1975, forty years after the household left Hertfordshire. That explains why a man in Johannesburg from the late 1930s to 1969 leaves so little in South African government series. Also new: she was married twice, formerly BAILEY. Checked and rejected along the way: "Wear, Martha" in Gazette 2438 of 20 June 1969 is MARTHA CUMMINGS WEAR, BORN CAMASK, of 17 Botha Avenue, Witbank, estate 6167/66 — not Martha Maud born Castle. Opened rather than trusted, which is now the rule.

rows.what: 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands — establish whether Leonard owned or rented it
rows.note: NEW, and it follows from the parents being at a DIFFERENT address on the same day. On 13 September 1969 Henry Robert Wear's household was a Parkhurst flat and L. A. R. Wear's was 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands. So the Fairlands address is Leonard's own, not a borrowed family one — which makes it worth testing in a way a family address would not be. A Deeds Office search on the erf will say whether he held title, and if he did it will say when he bought and WHEN HE SOLD OR DIED OUT OF IT, which bears directly on 1973 against 1979. Costs a search fee and needs somebody in Johannesburg; add to the held researcher brief rather than opening a correspondence.

rows.what: Folio F 3/8 — the possible transfer of the grave rights
rows.note: NEW and deliberately small. Row 4 of burial folio W 56 carries two lines in its Remarks column: "P. Fol. W.8.", which is the private-graves cross-reference and is certainly Wear's, and above it, in a smaller darker hand, "Transf. P.Fol. F 3/8." — a transfer of private rights to or from folio F 3/8. The ruling below both lines puts them in row 4's cell, but the page curves across two thousand pixels and the upper line may belong to row 3. THE ARCHIVE IS NOT CLAIMING IT. If it does belong to Wear then the grave rights in 56045 were transferred, and whoever they were transferred to is a name this archive does not have — which is the question row 57 asked and could not answer from the books it opened. Resolving it means finding the F-series folio in the same film and reading what grave it covers. One image, no fee. 15 September, partly answered without opening the F folio: the Private Graves Register HAS an "Authority to Purchase — Next of Kin" column and IT IS BLANK, for Wear and for six consecutive neighbouring rows (receipts 10997, 10999, 11009, 11475, 11484, 11517). The clerk on folio W 8 never used that column. So even had the 1986 reopening been recorded, the register's relationship field was not being filled in. The F 3/8 folio is still worth one image, but it is now the only thing this book can still give.

rows.what: Naturalisation file R54033, and whether Leonard ever had one
rows.note: NEW, and it is a record class this archive has never used. A gazette naturalisation notice is a name and an address; the FILE behind it records date and place of birth, previous nationality and PARENTS. Row 33 established that the South African civil marriage registers have no parentage field at all — this series does. Certificate R54033 was granted to Janette Eileen Maud Evans, nee Wear, on 30 October 1975; if the file names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle it is the first South African government record to state that couple as the parents of a child. It does not prove Leonard was theirs. THE SECOND QUESTION IS THE BIGGER ONE: ask in the same letter whether any naturalisation file exists for WEAR, Leonard Aubrey Robert, born 1917. A phrase search of the gazette returns nothing for him and no Wear in either the 1975 notice list or the 1976 grant list, but the lists are alphabetical and the OCR interleaves columns badly enough that this very entry had to be unpicked by hand — SO THAT NULL IS NOT AN ANSWER. Files for this period sit with the Department of Home Affairs, older series transferred to the National Archives, Pretoria. A letter, not a purchase. Send with the Master of the High Court business.

rows.what: The Bailey marriage — Janette Wear married twice
rows.note: NEW and small, but it is a free correction to the archive's own sibling table, which carries her as EVANS only. The 1975 gazette gives her as "formerly Bailey, nee Wear". So between the 1939 Register at Letchworth and 1975 she married a Bailey and then an Evans. A Bailey marriage is a dated document naming her father — if it was solemnised in England before she emigrated, the GRO marriage index will have it with the spouse's surname, and an English certificate DOES name fathers where the South African one does not. Order of work: GRO marriage index, WEAR, Janette E M, 1937 onwards, England and Wales. Cheap to search, about twelve pounds to buy if found, and David's call whether to buy.

rows.what: WLD 978/1960 — who was Mawthane Dabeah Kwele, and why was he suing Leonard
rows.note: NEW, and it is a fifth court file and a year the archive did not have. TAB, WLD 978/1960: ILLIQUID CASE, PAYMENT, MAWTHANE DABEAH KWELE VERSUS L A R WEAR. Leonard was in Johannesburg in 1960 and somebody sued him for money. The plaintiff's name is African, and a Black plaintiff bringing a payment action against a white defendant in the Witwatersrand Local Division in 1960 implies a working or trading relationship rather than a casual one — which would make this the only surviving trace of what Leonard actually DID for a living between the 1951 register's ENGINEER and the 1969 grave. The archive is not guessing further; the file would say. Add to the held researcher brief alongside the ante-nuptial contracts, since it is the same reading room.

rows.what: WLD 2961/1962 — the co-respondent named one number after the divorce
rows.note: NEW. WLD 2960/1962 is Marjorie Eileen Wear divorcing Leonard; WLD 2961/1962, filed one number later, is the same plaintiff suing ANOTHER WOMAN for DAMAGES. Same plaintiff, consecutive numbers, same year: in the practice of the period that is an action against the co-respondent, and it means the second marriage ended over somebody the archive has never heard of. HER NAME IS IN THE INDEX AND DELIBERATELY NOT ON THE SITE — she would be in her eighties or nineties if living, there is no death record for her, and the claim is an imputation of adultery drawn from two case numbers rather than from the file. Held in the private notes. What would settle it is the file itself, and it matters beyond gossip: a woman Leonard was involved with in 1962 is the likeliest person to have been near him in 1969, and 1969 is where he disappears.

rows.what: Ivone's naturalisation — the one route that names her parents on a South African form
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is a bounded negative that is itself a fact about her. The gazette was swept YEAR BY YEAR 1946-1980 for the forename Ivone — the search API takes a year filter and pages, which is how a common forename becomes tractable. Ten South African gazettes carry it in that window and EVERY ONE WAS OPENED: a Radium Station general dealer in 1951, Ivone da Conceicao Isaac in the 1962 grant list, Maria Ivone Freitas Basilio de Abreu of Emmarentia in 1967, Ivone Bertholet de Oliveira e Sousa Duran of Lourenco Marques in 1968, Maria Ivone Silva Almeida in the 1968 grant list, Maria Ivone Melo Gouveia in the 1970 list. NONE IS HER. The exact forms "Salkow, Ivone", "Ivone Salkow", "LUWINSKI, Ivone", "MOTA FIGUEIREDO" and "Rocha, Ivone" return zero each. IVONE DID NOT NATURALISE AS A SOUTH AFRICAN under any of her three surnames. The sweep also taught the format — surname, forenames, date of birth, country of birth, previous nationality, certificate number — and showed the lists FULL of Portuguese and Madeiran names through exactly the years she lived there. Other Portuguese naturalised steadily; she did not. That fits a woman who went back to Portugal and died at Porto, and it makes the Portuguese correspondence more important, not less.

rows.what: Da Rocha naturalisation — the father the family tree can only call Unknown
rows.note: DONE 15 September. "da Rocha, Henrique" and "Henrique Figueiredo Pinto" return three South African gazettes and ALL THREE ARE THE 2023 ESTATE NOTICES THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HAD for estate 12294/2023. No naturalisation notice, no grant. The route is closed and the father the tree calls Unknown is still unknown. What remains for him is the Portuguese military recenseamento, which is row 56, and the South African estate file itself.

rows.what: Salkow's naturalisation, and whether he was an immigrant at all
rows.note: DONE 15 September. "Salkow, Morris", "Morris Isaac Salkow" and "Salkow, Mrs" all return zero. The bare surname returns scores of hits across 1941-1969 but they are trade and business notices, not persons. No naturalisation for him either. Where Morris Isaac Salkow was born is still unestablished, and the gazette will not say.

rows.what: Cynthia Halsey's estate — a death notice naming Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle
rows.note: THE CLEANEST TEST AVAILABLE OF THE PARENTAL COUPLE. Row 33 established that the South African civil marriage registers have no parents' column at all, which is why the archive cannot document the Wear sibship from South African sources. But a DECEASED ESTATE does: form J294, the death notice, asks for the deceased's father's and mother's full names. Cynthia Yvonne Elizabeth Halsey, born Wear — her names in full from WLD 12617/78 — was Leonard's sister and divorced in 1978. FIND HER DEATH AND ORDER HER ESTATE. If its J294 names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, this archive at last has a South African government record stating that couple as the parents of a child. It does not prove Leonard was theirs; it removes the family tree as the only source for the couple.

rows.what: Janette Evans's estate — the same test, on a sister already proved dead
rows.note: Janette Eileen Maud Evans, formerly Bailey, born Wear, 28 October 1919 – 2001, is the best-documented of the siblings after tonight: GRO birth index, 1921 census, 1939 Register, the 1975 naturalisation notice, the 1976 certificate R54033, the 1977 divorce WLD 10428/77 and the South African verified deaths. SHE IS CERTAINLY DEAD, so no living-person question arises, and she died in 2001 — recent enough that the Master of the High Court will still hold the file. Its death notice names her parents. Run with row 65's sister-estate logic; whichever of the two is found first does the job.

rows.what: Martha Maud Wear's 1986 estate — outside the index, so it must be asked for
rows.note: Row 36 established that the NAAIRS deceased-estate index STOPS AT THE END OF 1976, so the absence of a 1986 estate proves nothing: it is out of range, not missing. Martha Maud Wear died 16 March 1986 aged 90, usual residence 12½ Second Street, Parkhurst, and was buried in her husband's grave. Her estate would be at the Master of the High Court, Johannesburg. Its death notice names HER parents — the Castle side — and its next-of-kin and heirs schedule lists her surviving children, WHICH IS THE LIST THIS ARCHIVE MOST WANTS. If Leonard predeceased her the schedule normally says so and often gives the date. Fold into the Master correspondence already running as row 2.

rows.what: The England and Wales probate calendar, 1970–1990, for Leonard
rows.note: WORKED 15 September to the end of what is free, and the result is a second instrument on which 1973 fails. The England and Wales probate service is free and its images ARE viewable without an account — but IT DOES NOT NAME-INDEX ANYTHING BEFORE 1996. A surname-and-year search returns scanned calendar pages and matches the string anywhere on the page, so WEAR also catches Weardale and Wearmouth. Searched with the keyword AUBREY to cut the noise: 1973 returns ZERO PAGES; then 8, 24, 19, 31, 13, 23, 19, 13 for 1974 to 1981. THE FAMILY TREE'S YEAR RETURNS NOTHING, on a second independent index, the evening after the South African estate index said the same. The 1979 pages have NOT been read — twenty-three dense calendar pages is an afternoon by eye, or minutes on a commercial index that has keyed the calendar by person. The row stays open and now says what it would cost.

rows.what: GRO consular and overseas death registrations for Leonard
rows.note: The second consequence of the family staying British. Deaths of British subjects abroad could be registered with a British consulate and appear in the GRO's Overseas Deaths indexes rather than in any South African series. That is a place this archive has never looked, and it is exactly where a man who was still legally British in the 1970s would land. Check the coverage first — registration was voluntary and many are missing — and publish the coverage dates alongside the result, so that a null is a bounded null and not a shrug. Feeds row 10.

rows.what: The GRO death index for England and Wales — in case he went home
rows.note: Third consequence. The archive has assumed Leonard died in South Africa because that is where it last saw him, in September 1969. He was a British subject with four siblings, at least one of whom was still shuttling between identities in 1975. A man of fifty-two, twice divorced, could have gone back. Search the GRO death index for WEAR, Leonard A R / Leonard Aubrey Robert, 1969 to 1990, and search it on the DATE OF BIRTH field where the index carries one — a 1917 birth at Hitchin is distinctive. Cheap, and the archive has never done it.

rows.what: Sweep every surname in the archive through NAAIRS, now that it can be driven
rows.note: Row 36 worked out how to drive the National Archives index programmatically — session token, the K0000001–K0000005 field names, the year range, and the &F=P print view that returns one clean document. The archive then used it for exactly two surnames. RUN THE WHOLE CAST: CASTLE, HALSEY, ROBERTSON, NORQUOY, DUNLOP, WALKER, MOMPLE, DE WITT, FIGUEIREDO, MOTA, SALKOW, DA ROCHA, LEIBHOLZ, HOSTOWSKY, BERNER, SEFTON, EISENHARDT, CRYSTAL, THORP, WILLIS, GANNON, CRIMES, GREEN, BAILEY, EVANS. Save every hit to a TSV the way the Figueiredo sweep was saved. This subsumes the South African half of row 39 and should be done before it.

rows.what: Fill the three null references in the litigation table from NAAIRS itself
rows.note: DONE 15 September. All six rows of litigation.json verified directly against NAAIRS rather than against a commercial mirror or a photograph of somebody's screen. TPD 534/1948 no longer needs its excuse: the index gives it in full — TAB, TPD, VOLUME 5/795, ILLIQUID CASE. DIVORCE. JOHANNES ANTONIE OELOFSE DE WITT VERSUS YVONNE (BORN DE FIGUEIREDO) — and THE VOLUME NUMBER IS NEW, which is what an order form actually needs. The nourl excuse is removed. And WLD 2545/1950 explains its own earlier obscurity: the index spells her IVONE LUWENSKI, not Luwinski, so a correct-spelling surname search could never have found it.

rows.what: The PIO immigration-papers series — Kurt's arrival, and everyone else's
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that KURT'S ARRIVAL IS NOT IN THE INDEX AT ALL. The PIO immigration series is real and indexed at item level, and it holds exactly one Wear and no Luwinski. KAB PIO 907, reference 38964E, IMMIGRATION PAPERS H C WEAR, 1949 — almost certainly not ours: the initials are H C, not H R or L A R, and 1949 is a decade after this archive dated the family's departure. Recorded because it is the only one and because "almost certainly not" should be written down rather than decided twice. Also found: KAB PIO 82445E, immigration papers re EISENHARDT, 1957. IMMIGRATION+LUWINSKI and PIO+LUWINSKI both return nothing. Kurt has no ship, no permit and no date, and the index that would hold them does not have him.

rows.what: Every WEAR burial at West Park, not just the two this archive stumbled on
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that LEONARD IS NOT THERE. Searched by collection rather than by guesswork — f.collectionId=4453927, the Johannesburg cemetery registers, 517 raw hits on the surname, collapsed to six distinct people: HENRIETTA WEAR buried 1909, HENRY ROBERT WEAR 13.9.1969, MARTHA MAUD WEAR 19.3.1986, EDWINA ANN WEAR 8.7.2014, MICHELLE ANN WEAR born 1978 died 27.3.2017, and DAN B WEAR undated. He bought grave 56045 and he was not buried in it, and he is in no other Johannesburg cemetery register the collection indexes. BOUNDS: this is the INDEXED layer of ONE collection covering 1840-2019; it does not cover unindexed images in it, other Johannesburg cemeteries, or the Chevrah Kadisha, which is a separate database — a Wear would have no business in a Jewish cemetery but the exclusion is stated rather than assumed. TWO WEARS ARE NEW: Michelle Ann Wear, born 1978, the right age to be a granddaughter of Bruce Wallace Wear who married four times; and Dan B Wear. Both written down, neither pursued.

rows.what: Grave 56045 — is there a stone, and what is carved on it
rows.note: Two people are in that grave and a third person paid sixty pounds for it. A private grave of 1969 in section E.C. would ordinarily carry a memorial, and the burial register has a Remarks column headed "Private Rights, MEMORIALS" in which other rows on the same page record memorials erected and their cost. A photograph of the stone would say who is commemorated and, if a family stone, possibly who paid for it and when it was last added to. Ask the City of Johannesburg cemeteries office, or any of the local volunteer photographers who work West Park. Costs nothing but a request.

rows.what: The undertakers — Cooks in 1969 and REG in 1986
rows.note: Row 57 established that the cemetery books do not record who authorised the 1986 reopening, because a second interment into an existing private grave generated no grave transaction at all. But SOMEBODY instructed the undertaker, and the register names them: Cooks for Henry Robert in September 1969, REG for Martha Maud in March 1986. An undertaker's own file records the informant — the person who arranged and paid for the funeral — with their name, address and relationship to the deceased. Identify both firms, establish whether either still exists or whether its records went to a repository, and ask. This is the last route to the 1986 authority.

rows.what: The five Wear court files, as a set, from the Transvaal depot
rows.note: The archive now knows of five and has read none: WLD 2026/1951 (Phyllis v Leonard, divorce), WLD 790/1957 (Leonard v Norquoy, opposed application), WLD 978/1960 (Kwele v L A R Wear, payment), WLD 2960/1962 (Marjorie v Leonard, divorce) and WLD 2961/1962 (Marjorie v a named woman, damages). A divorce summons of the period recites BOTH PARTIES' FULL NAMES, AGES, DOMICILES AND THE DATE AND PLACE OF THE MARRIAGE, and often the children by name and birth date. Five files from one depot on one visit; the researcher is already holding a brief for the ante-nuptial contracts and this belongs in the same envelope. Supersedes the separate handling of rows 63 and 64.

rows.what: Does a South African marriage register after 1970 have a parents' column?
rows.note: Row 33's finding was bounded: the civil marriage register never asked for parents between 1940 and 1970, across two form designs. NOBODY HAS CHECKED WHETHER THE FORM CHANGED AFTERWARDS. There are now three post-1970 Wear marriages to test it on — Bruce Wallace Wear's to Margaret Gannon (divorced WLD 489/77), his to Edwina Ann Green in 1980, and whatever Janette's Evans marriage was. If a 1970s or 1980s form carries a parents' column, then every later marriage in this family becomes a parentage document and row 33's conclusion needs its date range narrowed in public.

rows.what: Phyllis Agnes Robertson — the Norquoy marriage of 14 June 1952, and what became of her
rows.note: ADVANCED 15 September — a candidate name, from NAAIRS. Phyllis remarried a Norquoy on 14 June 1952 and Leonard sued "Phyllis Agnes Norquoy" in 1957. NAAIRS holds fourteen Norquoy documents and two are a Johannesburg man in exactly the right years: WLD 1198/1957, Edward William Allen versus ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY, and TPD 1624/1960, Sadi Jacobs versus Robert Selwyn Norquoy. ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY IS VERY PROBABLY HER SECOND HUSBAND — rare Orkney surname, right city, right decade, and WLD 1198/1957 filed the same year as Leonard's WLD 790/1957 against her. Stated as an inference from surname, place and date; no document yet joins them. Next: the 1952 marriage register under the name Norquoy, and his estate. There is no Norquoy estate for a Phyllis Agnes in the index, but the index stops in 1976 and she may have outlived it.

rows.what: Marjorie Eileen Walker, formerly Dunlop — Leonard's second wife
rows.note: She married him in October 1951 at Polana Court, Abel Road, Berea, divorced him in 1962, and sued another woman for damages one case number later. She had been married before, to a Dunlop. She is the person who knew Leonard best in the years the archive cannot see, and she is untraced. Find her death and her estate. A woman who litigated twice in one year kept paperwork, and an estate file is where it survives.

rows.what: Insolvency and sequestration notices for L. A. R. Wear
rows.note: He was sued for payment in 1960 and this archive has taken that as an isolated fact. The Government Gazette publishes sequestrations and insolvencies with a rigour nothing else in this record has: SURNAME, FULL FORENAMES, OCCUPATION, RESIDENTIAL ADDRESS, and in many notices the DATE OF BIRTH and identity number. If Leonard was ever sequestrated, that notice is the single most informative line about him in existence. Search the estate and insolvency notices for WEAR with the initials L A R, and for the Fairlands and Berea addresses.

rows.what: What happened to the Piccadilly Hat Company after 1952
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the shop had a life before Kurt. The 1940 page was unreadable in OCR, so the PDF page was rendered at 200 dpi and read as an image. Government Gazette 2825 of 8 November 1940, page VII: NOTICE OF SALE OF BUSINESS — "The business of PICCADILLY HAT SHOP carried on by PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PROPRIETARY), LIMITED, at HANNAH COURT, 81 ELOFF STREET, Johannesburg, has been sold and will be transferred to IVY FUCHS, a public trader, who will carry on the said business under the same style or firm at the same address for her own account and benefit as from the 1st of October, 1940." Attorney Israel Katz, Sauer's Buildings. THREE GAINS: the building is named — HANNAH COURT, which this archive did not have; the shop belonged to a company, PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PTY) LTD; and KURT BOUGHT IT FROM A NAMED PREDECESSOR, IVY FUCHS, who had held it for thirteen months. He bought a going concern with a history, not an empty name. Also found: 16 May 1952 no. 4846 lists "Piccadilly Hat Co." in a registration schedule under VCR. 429/8/49, a 1949 registration.

rows.what: Pauline Luwinski's estate — Kurt's widow, died 1985
rows.note: She survived Kurt by seventeen years, was the sequestrating creditor against Phillip Crystal in 1972, traded as Pallou's Dress Centre at 18 Wanderers Street in 1975, and is buried at Westpark, grave V-1470. Her estate is past the NAAIRS cut-off of 1976 and so must be asked for from the Master. Its death notice names HER parents, and its heirs schedule records who was alive in 1985 and what they received — which is the nearest thing to a family list the Luwinski side will ever produce.

rows.what: Read the FamilySearch catalogue at item level, not the browse labels
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the technique transferred but the target did not need it. The catalogue search is /service/search/catalog/v3/search?q.keywords=..., whose replies come back as searchHits[].metadataHit.metadata — not the shape the sister archive's parser expected — and the item call is /service/search/catalog/item/<id>. Applied to Johannesburg it finds olib:4453927, "South Africa, Johannesburg, cemetery registers: COLLECTION RECORD, 1840-2019", and the item record says plainly NOT AVAILABLE ON MICROFILM: it is a digital-image collection, so there is no film_note list of volumes to read and the browse-label problem the technique was invented to solve does not arise here. WHAT REPLACES IT IS BETTER: the collection has an id, and the persona search takes f.collectionId, which turns "every Wear in Johannesburg's cemeteries" into one query. That is how row 77 was answered. NOTE A DISCREPANCY WORTH KNOWING: the item's own summary says the collection holds Olifantsvlei registers 2017-2021 while its title says 1840-2019. The title is right — the 1969 and 1986 West Park entries are in it — so THE SUMMARY IS WRONG, and anyone reading the catalogue description alone would wrongly conclude this collection cannot help them.

rows.what: Run the FamilySearch full-text search over the unindexed South African images
rows.note: Everything this archive has found on FamilySearch has come through the indexed name search or through images it knew to open. FamilySearch now runs full text over images that were never indexed, which is a different instrument: it reads the handwriting on pages nobody catalogued. Run WEAR with LEONARD, LUWINSKI, and MOTA FIGUEIREDO against the South African collections. The cemetery register that broke row 55 open was found by opening images by hand; this is the same act done at scale.

rows.what: Digitised Johannesburg directories and voters rolls — establish which are reachable from here
rows.note: Row 41 closed with the judgement that street directories, the Deeds Office index and the voters rolls "all need somebody physically in Johannesburg or Pretoria". That was asserted rather than checked. Some South African directories and voters rolls are digitised on the commercial sites and on the National Library's portal. Establish EXACTLY which years of the Johannesburg directory and which voters rolls are reachable without a reading room, and write the list down. If even one year between 1942 and 1950 is online, it goes straight at the nine-year hole that row 41 could not fill.

rows.what: A register of bounded negatives — what has been searched and did not exist
rows.note: DONE 15 September — /negatives/ is live and in the navigation. Nine bounded negatives, each with three columns: WHAT WAS SEARCHED, WHAT CAME BACK, AND WHAT WOULD STILL FALL OUTSIDE IT. The last column is the point. It holds the distinction between "this is not there", which is a finding, and "I did not find it", which is a shrug. The page also records the two nulls this archive produced by its own error in one evening — a grid read before its async postback had landed, and a form field posted with an empty value — both of which looked exactly like an empty holding and neither of which was. The rule it enforces: do not publish a null you did not bound.

rows.what: Maud Mabel Castle of Johannesburg — coincidence, or the reason the family went there
rows.note: NEW, out of row 39, and deliberately framed as a test rather than a claim. A Maud born Castle was divorcing an Aubrey Leonard Longhurst in Johannesburg in 1915 and again in 1919, two years before Martha Maud Castle bore a son she christened Leonard Aubrey. Martha Maud cannot be that woman — she was nineteen and in Hertfordshire — but a relative could be, and if she was, the archive gains the thing it has never had: A REASON WHY THIS FAMILY CROSSED TO THAT PARTICULAR CITY. Emigrating families go where somebody already is, and the Wear emigration has always been a bare fact with no pull behind it. Three cheap tests, in order: (1) GRO and censuses for a MAUD MABEL CASTLE born in the 1880s in Hertfordshire or Bedfordshire, and whether she sits in the same household or parish as Martha Maud's family at Baldock; (2) MHG 3632/50, Aubrey Leonard Longhurst's estate of 1950, which is INSIDE the estate index's range and orderable, and whose death notice names his parents; (3) WLD 155/1915, whose summons would recite the date and place of the first marriage. If all three come back negative, say so on the bounded-negatives page and close it.
